extracted.intended_audience: USPTO policymakers, patent examiners, patent practitioners (attorneys/agents), and other stakeholders considering restriction/unity of invention reform
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluation and proposed procedures for changing U.S. patent restriction practice toward a unity-of-invention-style standard (including multiple Options, fee structures, examiner procedures, and transition/corrective mechanisms). Intended to guide policy decisions and implementation details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Option 2 — Modified PCT 'unity of invention' standard
rubrics_metrics.description: The current PCT 'unity of invention' standard, modified to require that any purported special technical/common feature comply with 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph, would be applied to all US applications. Applicants would be given the option of concurrent examination of multiple inventions that lack unity of invention for an additional fee.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unity exists only when there is a technical relationship among the claimed inventions involving one or more of the same or corresponding 'special technical features' that define a contribution which each invention makes over the prior art. Whether a technical feature makes a 'contribution' should be considered with respect to prior art and 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph (support/enablement). If the examiner can demonstrate lack of support for the main claim, there is no technical relationship. Applicants may be invited to identify a reference claim to determine relationships in applications with many inventions. Feedback: implementation/examination under Option 2 considered more difficult than Option 1 but less difficult than Options 3 or 4.

rubrics_metrics.name: Option 3 — 'related or unrelated' standard with three-tiered fee structure
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'related or unrelated' standard involving a three-tiered fee structure dependent upon search burden and the presence of different patentability issues between various inventions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Process: examiner first identifies 'inventions' using current independent/distinct standard; applicant elects one invention as reference and indicates whether to place remaining inventions into tiers; examiner places inventions into tiers; applicant indicates whether they will pay for examination of additional inventions. This additional decision increases process length and decreases predictability. Feedback: implementation/examination under Option 3 considered much more difficult than Option 1.

rubrics_metrics.name: Option 4 — Require inventions subject to restriction be both 'independent and distinct' (reinterpretation of 35 U.S.C. 112)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reinterpret 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph to require that inventions subject to restriction be both 'independent and distinct.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This may involve identification of a common feature; if applicant does not identify it, the examiner must identify it and applicant may rebut. If multiple groupings with distinct common features exist, applicant must elect a single grouping and invention within that grouping. May involve 'rolling' searches of the common feature or additional inventions. Proposal includes charging a single additional fee in all applications where a restriction/election is made and the inventions include at least one common feature. Feedback: implementation/examination under Option 4 considered the most difficult and significantly more difficult than current practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Option 1 — Current 'independent or distinct' standard with option to pay for additional inventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Retain current 35 U.S.C. §121 'independent or distinct' standard and give applicants the option to request and pay for examination of up to 2 additional distinct or independent inventions beyond current practice; option to request/pay for up to 10 species per invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Methodology for study: review applications under current restriction practice post-election; record groups categorized as distinct or independent; record species (Markush vs non-Markush). Concurrent examination limited to species within lowest level of nested Markush groups. Feedback: Option 1 considered least difficult among options studied.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition — 'Independent' inventions
rubrics_metrics.description: The term 'independent' means there is no disclosed relationship between the two or more subjects disclosed; they are unconnected in design, operation, or effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: (1) species under a genus which are not usable together as disclosed; (2) process and apparatus incapable of being used in practicing the process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition — 'Distinct' inventions
rubrics_metrics.description: The term 'distinct' means two or more subjects as disclosed are related (e.g., combination and part/subcombination, process and apparatus for its practice, process and product made) but are capable of separate manufacture, use, or sale as claimed, and are patentable (novel and unobvious) over each other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: They may each be unpatentable over the prior art yet still be 'distinct' relative to each other for restriction purposes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition — 'Species' counting and Markush rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Species are categorized as part of a Markush group or not; the number of species in a Markush group was recorded (up to 100 members). For genus claims found patentable, the species covered by that genus counted as a single species.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concurrent examination limited to species within the lowest level of any nested Markush groups (example: if 10 formulas each have 100 species, applicants may elect to pay for examination of 10 species from one formula only). For non-Markush species, the examiner does not specify claims in the restriction requirement; applicant must specify elected claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiner use of a reference claim for determining relationship among claims
rubrics_metrics.description: In applications with many inventions, applicant will be invited to identify a reference claim for determination of the relationship of remaining claims (i.e., whether they contain 'the same or corresponding special technical/common feature(s)').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reference-claim procedure used where necessary (particularly in chemical and biotechnology applications) to determine relatedness among many inventions; see Development of Restriction Standard Options for the Study.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fee proposal for examination of additional inventions and species
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposed fees to have applicants who benefit from concurrent examination bear associated costs: additional search fee ($500) and examination fee ($200) per additional invention paid at the time applicant chooses examination; up to 10 species per invention at $250 per species; no additional filing fee; issue fee charged for each additional invention at allowance; separate maintenance fees for each additional invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Office proposed mirroring current fee schedule to simplify implementation; fees indicated are those provided under newly enacted fee legislation. Any fee schedule should maintain revenue stream equivalent to FY06 budget estimate; public comments generally preferred that applicants who benefit pay associated costs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impact assessment — output and pendency metrics
rubrics_metrics.description: Estimate of how each Option would affect examiner production (output), pendency (first action pendency), and the number of divisional/RCE/continuation filings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Study provided numeric estimates (e.g., production units lost cumulative FY2005-2010 for Option 1 and 2 variations; increases in first action pendency in months e.g., Option1 1 extra = 4.0 months, Option1 2 extra = 5.6 months, etc.). Effects vary significantly by Technology Center (e.g., TC1600 severely impacted). Concurrent examination could reduce divisional filings (assumed 50% reduction) but increase RCE/Continuation filings, potentially offsetting benefits. If Office cannot hire sufficient examiners, output reduced and pendency increased relative to FY06 budget.

rubrics_metrics.name: FTE and cost estimates to maintain pendency targets
rubrics_metrics.description: Estimate of number of additional examiner Full Time Employees (FTEs) needed and associated salary/benefit costs for FY2005–FY2010 to maintain pendency under Options 1 and 2.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Option1, 1 extra: 1,220 FTEs ($226,468,700 salary/benefits); Option1, 2 extra: 1,520 FTEs ($293,329,534); Option2 numbers also provided. Additional costs not reflected include computers, furniture, space, administrative costs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Revenue impact and need to revise fee schedule
rubrics_metrics.description: Adoption of Options 1 or 2 would reduce output and therefore reduce revenue (fewer allowances and maintenance fees). A revised fee schedule would be needed to generate the same annual revenue stream as indicated in the FY06 budget estimate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Study provided lost revenue figures (cumulative lost revenue FY2005-2010 per option). Office suggested mirroring current fee schedule and making applicants who benefit bear associated costs; several approaches to fee increases enumerated (increase filing fees, add fee for examination of claims lacking unity, increase issue/maintenance fees generally or only for payers).

rubrics_metrics.name: Partial search vs assessing 35 U.S.C. §112 when lack of unity arises
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether to perform only a 'partial search' when examination of entire scope of claims is unduly burdensome due to non-prior-art issues, or to assess adequacy of disclosure and industrial applicability (35 U.S.C. §112 issues) in addition to prior art when determining whether claimed common feature makes a contribution over the prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some international authorities make 'partial search' declarations in such circumstances; the USPTO historically does not. Public comments expressed mixed support for partial search and less support to look to §112 issues in making lack of unity determinations, though some organizations favored considering non-prior art issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Whether to adopt EPO (central claiming) practices (one independent claim per category and emphasis on independent claims)
rubrics_metrics.description: Question whether USPTO should study adopting EPO claim treatment practice (normally allowing only one independent claim per category of invention and emphasizing search/examination of independent claims), and whether to modify examination of dependent claims and consider changes to presumption of validity under 35 U.S.C. 282.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public comments showed no consensus and generally strong objection to moving to EPO-style claim drafting/search/treatment. Consideration must account for differences in US practice (USPTO searches/examines every claim and every limitation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Practice on examining first claimed invention vs applicant election (PCT-style)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether to adopt the PCT practice of examining the first claimed invention when lack of unity is held, or to allow applicant opportunity to elect an invention to be examined (or examine first claimed product vs first claimed invention).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public comments generally encouraged retaining oral elections and some limited support for examining the first claimed invention if applicant fails to orally elect; preference to keep current practice of written requirement if oral election not possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Work assignment and examination quality safeguards
rubrics_metrics.description: How work should be assigned to ensure examination quality when multiple inventions crossing disciplines must be examined in a single application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Options for maintaining quality include (1) team examination (EPO-style three-person divisions), (2) extending use of patentability report procedures (MPEP §705), (3) maintaining the single-examiner model, or (4) other hybrid options. Public comments generally preferred continuing single-examiner model and recommending team examination case-by-case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of RCE authority to permit post-prosecution submission/examination of additional inventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Use 35 U.S.C. 132(b) authority to permit applicants to pay an RCE fee and submit or rejoin claims to additional inventions after prosecution closed on first invention, provided submitted claims depend from or include features of allowed claims that make a contribution over the prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such an option would allow continued examination under a Unity standard without statutory change; questions include whether to limit availability to published applications and how to set RCE fee relative to current fee structure. Public comments generally expressed strong opposition, possibly due to misunderstanding of the scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of continued examination to permit requests to continue examination of withdrawn claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Permit requests that the USPTO continue examination of claims withdrawn from consideration by requiring applicants to request continued examination, pay a fee for treatment of one additional invention, and present claims drawn only to that additional invention (available in addition to filing a divisional).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public comments expressed mixed support for this proposed procedure. Considerations include how to offset loss in issue and maintenance fee collections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transition protocol for applying any new restriction standard
rubrics_metrics.description: If a new restriction standard is adopted, apply it only to applications filed on or after the effective date and to pending applications that had not received a first action on the merits prior to the effective date; request for treatment under the new standard permitted with either filing an RCE or refiling the application where a first action was issued prior to the effective date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This transition protocol seeks to avoid rework of efforts already expended in examination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corrective petition process similar to PCT Rule 40.2(c)
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide a petition process similar to the PCT protest provisions under PCT Rule 40.2(c) if a revised restriction procedure that permits applicants to request and pay for examination of additional inventions is adopted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This would create a formal corrective mechanism to challenge restriction/election determinations under the revised process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public/user impacts — practitioner strategy and claim drafting consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: A revised restriction standard will require practitioners to become familiar with new filing and prosecution strategies; options to pay for immediate examination of additional inventions would affect whether practitioners request immediate examination or wait and file divisionals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decisions must be made prior to search and examination and therefore with limited patentability information. Claim drafting styles may need reconsideration; e.g., inclusion of purported same or corresponding special technical/common feature in independent claims may prove valuable under Option 2.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stakeholder preference to address consistency before statutory change
rubrics_metrics.description: Public comments generally provided strong input that the Office should first address consistency in current procedures and then determine if further changes are needed; balance cost and impact on quality before changing statute or procedure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some comments suggested seeking authority to permit applicants either to file additional divisionals or seek examination of related inventions in a single case with fee-setting authority to recover costs; others suggested overhaul of production incentives that encourage undue restriction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Survey feedback difficulty ranking of Options
rubrics_metrics.description: Survey feedback indicated relative difficulty of implementing/examining under the options: Option 1 least difficult; Option 2 more difficult than Option 1 but less so than Options 3 and 4; Option 3 much more difficult than Option 1; Option 4 most difficult.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these perceived difficulty rankings as an input to decisions about feasibility, implementation complexity, training needs, and likely impact on predictability and pendency.
